text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
--State shareholdings in a number of companies, particularly in North Sea oil and gas, contributed earnings of 952 million crowns to government coffers in 1996, 100 million more than the year before.
--The jurists and economists pension fund has sold its shares in French oil company Total, because of its widespread investments in military-ruled Burma.

--The planned sale of 48 percent of shipbuilder Danyard Research shows that consumers want a wider range of products and shops to choose between and are preapered to drive to larger shopping areas in order to find it, but the environment ministry seeks to limit the amount of shop space in large towns, to encourage trade in smaller communities.

--A survey shows that 7,000 Danish companies are under-capitalised, mainly because they are reluctant to cede to investors the influence that goes with a shareholding. The survey of 80,000 firms said that the result is that companies must often close, rather than grow, for lack of development capital.

--Major insurance companies expect to reap a bonanza from companies growing social programmes. Firms see it as cost-effective and encouraging staff loyalty to send employers to private hospitals rather than have them wait for treatment at public institutions, to offer them alchol-abuse treatment or to guarantee them financial security in the event of serious illness.
--Jyske Bank is to write off the debts of its customers who borrowed to buy summer-houses for commercial letting in what transpired to be an illegal scheme.

--Human rights group Amnesty International, often a critic of multinationals' behaviour in the developing world, is building bridges to Danish industry and is to launch its new Business Club in autumn to improve ties.
